question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the absolute value equation 

$$
-8|2x+1|+20=4.
$$

This equation can be expressed in the following equivalent form:

$|2x+1|=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We can rearrange the equation to isolate the absolute value on the left side:

First, we subtract $20$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-8|2x+1|+20 & =4 \\ -8|2x+1|+20-20 & =4-20 \\ -8|2x+1| & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $-8:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8|2x+1| & =-16 \\ \frac{-8|2x+1|}{-8} & =\frac{-16}{-8} \\ \frac{\cancel{-8}|2x+1|}{\cancel{-8}} & =2 \\ |2x+1| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the absolute value equation 

$$
5-|x-3|=-3.
$$

This equation can be expressed in the following equivalent form:

$$
|x-3|=k
$$

What is the value of $k?$
question.worked_solution:
We can rearrange the equation to isolate the absolute value on the left side:

First, we subtract $5$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5-|x-3|=-3 \\ 5-|x-3|-5=-3-5 \\ -|x-3|=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-|x-3| & =-8 \\ (-1)\cdot (-|x-3|) & =(-1)\cdot (-8) \\ (\cancel{-}1)\cdot (\cancel{-}|x-3|) & =8 \\ |x-3| & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=8.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Which of the following equations has *no* solution?

I. $|2x+1|-2=3$

II. $|2x+1|=1$

III. $|2x+1|=-3$
question.worked_solution:
An absolute value equation has no solution if, when the absolute value is isolated on the left side, the right-hand side is negative.

With that in mind, let's look at each equation in turn:

- Equation I has a solution. To see this, we first isolate the absolute value on the left-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x+1|-2 & =3 \\ |2x+1| & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-hand side is non-negative, this equation has a solution.

- Equation II has a solution. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is non-negative.

- Equation III *has no solution*. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is *negative*.

Therefore, the answer is "III only."

question.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5-x|-8 & =7 \\ |5-x| & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|5-x|=5-x,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5-x| & =15 \\ 5-x & =15 \\ -x & =10 \\ x & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|5-x|=-(5-x),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5-x| & =15 \\ -(5-x) & =15 \\ -5+x & =15 \\ x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the solutions are $x=-10$ and $x=20.$

$$

$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Rearranging and Solving an Absolute Value Equation
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2|5x-3|+1 & =15 \\ 2|5x-3| & =14 \\ |5x-3| & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|5x-3|=5x-3,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5x-3| & =7 \\ 5x-3 & =7 \\ 5x & =10 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|5x-3|=-(5x-3),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5x-3| & =7 \\ -(5x-3) & =7 \\ -5x+3 & =7 \\ -5x & =4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ and $x=2.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

If 2|5x−3|+1=15, then x=

a
x=−2,45
b
x=−2,−45
c
x=−25,2
d
x=−45,2
e
x=45,2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation: 2|5x−3|+1=152|5x−3|=14|5x−3|=7

Now, we have the following two cases:

  • If |5x−3|=5x−3, we obtain: |5x−3|=75x−3=75x=10x=2

  • If |5x−3|=−(5x−3), we obtain: |5x−3|=7−(5x−3)=7−5x+3=7−5x=4x=−45

Therefore, the solutions are x=−45 and x=2.
question.knowledge_point: Rearranging and Solving an Absolute Value Equation

solution.reasoning: Subtracting 1 and dividing by 2 gives |5x-3|=7. Thus 5x-3=-7 or 5x-3=7, yielding x=-4/5 or x=2, option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation: 2|5x−3|+1=152|5x−3|=14|5x−3|=7

Now, we have the following two cases:

  • If |5x−3|=5x−3, we obtain: |5x−3|=75x−3=75x=10x=2

  • If |5x−3|=−(5x−3), we obtain: |5x−3|=7−(5x−3)=7−5x+3=7−5x=4x=−45

Therefore, the solutions are x=−45 and x=2.

question.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6-2b|+2 & =18 \\ |6-2b| & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|6-2b|=6-2b,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6-2b| & =16 \\ 6-2b & =16 \\ -2b & =10 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|6-2b|=-(6-2b),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6-2b| & =16 \\ -(6-2b) & =16 \\ 2b-6 & =16 \\ 2b & =22 \\ b & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $b=-5$ and $b=11.$

question.html:
Question 10
?

If |6−2b|+2=18, then b=

a
b=5,11
b
b=−11,5
c
b=−5,11
d
b=−5,12
e
b=−12,3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation: |6−2b|+2=18|6−2b|=16

Now, we have the following two cases:

  • If |6−2b|=6−2b, we obtain: |6−2b|=166−2b=16−2b=10b=−5

  • If |6−2b|=−(6−2b), we obtain: |6−2b|=16−(6−2b)=162b−6=162b=22b=11

Therefore, the solutions are b=−5 and b=11.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: If $17y=9y-16$, then $y=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $17y$ on the left-hand side and $9y$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the left-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $9y$ from the right-hand side. We do this by subtracting $9y$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}17y & =9y-16 \\ 17y-9y & =9y-16-9y \\ 8y & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $8:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8y & =-16 \\ \frac{8y}{8} & =\frac{(-16)}{8} \\ \frac{\cancel{8}y}{\cancel{8}} & =-2 \\ y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that $2x+6=5x$, what is the value of $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $2x$ on the left-hand side and $5x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side. 

The first step is to remove the $2x$ from the left-hand side. We do this by subtracting $2x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+6 & =5x \\ 2x+6-2x & =5x-2x \\ 6 & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3x \\ \frac{6}{3} & =\frac{3x}{3} \\ 2 & =\frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} \\ 2 & =x \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: If $10x-3=5+6x,$ then $x=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $10x$ on the left-hand side and $6x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the left-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $6x$ from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting $6x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-3 & =5+6x \\ 10x-3-6x & =5+6x-6x \\ 4x-3 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-3$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding $3$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-3 & =5 \\ 4x-3+3 & =5+3 \\ 4x & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =8 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & =\frac{8}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} & =2 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses on both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}7(x-2) & =3(x+2)+2x \\ 7\cdot x-7\cdot 2 & =3\cdot x+3\cdot 2+2x \\ 7x-14 & =3x+6+2x \\ 7x-14 & =6+3x+2x \\ 7x-14 & =6+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $7x$ on the left-hand side and $5x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $5x$ from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting $5x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-14 & =6+5x \\ 7x-14-5x & =6+5x-5x \\ 2x-14 & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-14$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding $14$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-14 & =6 \\ 2x-14+14 & =6+14 \\ 2x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =20 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{20}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & =10 \\ x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $12 - 5m = 3m$, what is the value of $m?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $-5m$ on the left-hand side and $3m$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $-5m$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding ${\color{blue}5m}$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}12-5m & =3m \\ 12-5m+5m & =3m+5m \\ 12 & =8m\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $8\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =8m \\ \frac{12}{8} & =\frac{8m}{8} \\ \frac{3}{2} & =\frac{\cancel{8}m}{\cancel{8}} \\ \frac{3}{2} & =m \\ m & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $3x$ on the left-hand side and $5x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $3x$ from the left-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting ${\color{blue}3x}$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-12 & =5x+8 \\ 3x-12-3x & =5x+8-3x \\ -12 & =2x+8\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $8$ from the right-hand side. We do this by subtracting ${\color{red}8}$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =2x+8 \\ -12-8 & =2x+8-8 \\ -20 & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-20 & =2x \\ \frac{-20}{2} & =\frac{2x}{2} \\ -10 & =\frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} \\ -10 & =x \\ x & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Solve for $t$ where $2(t+3)= 5t-3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses on the left-hand-side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t+3) & =5t-3 \\ 2\cdot t+2\cdot 3 & =5t-3 \\ 2t+6 & =5t-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must now bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $2t$ on the left-hand side and $5t$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $2t$ from the left-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting ${\color{blue}2t}$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+6 & =5t-3 \\ 2t+6-2t & =5t-3-2t \\ 6 & =3t-3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-3$ from the right-hand side. We do this by adding ${\color{red}3}$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3t-3 \\ 6+3 & =3t-3+3 \\ 9 & =3t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =3t \\ \frac{9}{3} & =\frac{3t}{3} \\ 3 & =\frac{\cancel{3}t}{\cancel{3}} \\ 3 & =t \\ t & =3\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To solve a linear equation with variables on both sides, we bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

For example, let's solve the following equation: 

$$
5x = 2x + 12
$$

 

Notice that we have $5x$ on the left-hand side and $2x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the left-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $\color{blue}2x$ from the right-hand side. We can do this by *subtracting* it from both sides of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & =2x+12 \\ 5x-2x & =2x+12-2x \\ 3x & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =12 \\ \frac{3x}{3} & =\frac{12}{3} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} & =4 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=4$ is our answer, and we're done. 

We can check that $x=4$ is correct by substituting back into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & \overset{?}{=}2x+12 \\ 5(4) & \overset{?}{=}2(4)+12 \\ 20 & =20\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now solve the following equation: 

$$
9x -9= 1+4x
$$

To solve this equation, we must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $9x$ on the left-hand side and $4x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the left-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $4x$ from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting ${\color{blue}4x}$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}9x-9 & =1+4x \\ 9x-9-4x & =1+4x-4x \\ 5x-9 & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-9$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding ${\color{red}9}$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-9 & =1 \\ 5x-9+9 & =1+9 \\ 5x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & =10 \\ \frac{5x}{5} & =\frac{10}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & =2 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=2$ is our answer. We can check that this is correct by substituting back into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9x-9 & =1+4x \\ 9(2)-9 & \overset{?}{=}1+4(2) \\ 18-9 & \overset{?}{=}9 \\ 9 & =9\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.problem:
Let's now solve the following equation: 

$$
9x -9= 1+4x
$$

To solve this equation, we must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $9x$ on the left-hand side and $4x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the left-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $4x$ from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting ${\color{blue}4x}$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}9x-9 & =1+4x \\ 9x-9-4x & =1+4x-4x \\ 5x-9 & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-9$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding ${\color{red}9}$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-9 & =1 \\ 5x-9+9 & =1+9 \\ 5x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & =10 \\ \frac{5x}{5} & =\frac{10}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & =2 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=2$ is our answer. We can check that this is correct by substituting back into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9x-9 & =1+4x \\ 9(2)-9 & \overset{?}{=}1+4(2) \\ 18-9 & \overset{?}{=}9 \\ 9 & =9\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $2x+6=5x$, what is the value of $x?$
question.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $2x$ on the left-hand side and $5x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side. 

The first step is to remove the $2x$ from the left-hand side. We do this by subtracting $2x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+6 & =5x \\ 2x+6-2x & =5x-2x \\ 6 & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3x \\ \frac{6}{3} & =\frac{3x}{3} \\ 2 & =\frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} \\ 2 & =x \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Two-Step Equations
last_observation.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $2x$ on the left-hand side and $5x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side. 

The first step is to remove the $2x$ from the left-hand side. We do this by subtracting $2x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+6 & =5x \\ 2x+6-2x & =5x-2x \\ 6 & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3x \\ \frac{6}{3} & =\frac{3x}{3} \\ 2 & =\frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} \\ 2 & =x \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: If $10x-3=5+6x,$ then $x=${{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $10x$ on the left-hand side and $6x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the left-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $6x$ from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting $6x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-3 & =5+6x \\ 10x-3-6x & =5+6x-6x \\ 4x-3 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-3$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding $3$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-3 & =5 \\ 4x-3+3 & =5+3 \\ 4x & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =8 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & =\frac{8}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} & =2 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: If $-4-3t=3t-2,$ then $t=${{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
We must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $-3t$ on the left-hand side and $3t$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $-3t$ from the left-hand side of the equation. We do this by adding $3t$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4-3t & =3t-2 \\ -4-3t+3t & =3t-2+3t \\ -4 & =6t-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-2$ from the right-hand side. We do this by adding $2$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =6t-2 \\ -4+2 & =6t-2+2 \\ -2 & =6t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $6:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =6t \\ \frac{(-2)}{6} & =\frac{6t}{6} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\cancel{6}t}{\cancel{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & =t \\ t & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

If −3(1−p)=4(p+1), then p=

a
−16
b
−7
c
−14
d
34
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we expand the parentheses on both sides: −3(1−p)=4(p+1)−3⋅1+3⋅p=4⋅p+4⋅1−3+3p=4p+4

Now, we must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side.

Notice that we have 3p on the left-hand side and 4p on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the 3p from the left-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting 3p from both sides: −3+3p=4p+4−3+3p−3p=4p+4−3p−3=p+4

Finally, we remove the 4 from the right-hand side. We do this by subtracting 4 from both sides:

−3=p+4−3−4=p+4−4−7=pp=−7

question.name: Question 6
question.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses on both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}7(x-2) & =3(x+2)+2x \\ 7\cdot x-7\cdot 2 & =3\cdot x+3\cdot 2+2x \\ 7x-14 & =3x+6+2x \\ 7x-14 & =6+3x+2x \\ 7x-14 & =6+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $7x$ on the left-hand side and $5x$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the $5x$ from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting $5x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-14 & =6+5x \\ 7x-14-5x & =6+5x-5x \\ 2x-14 & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-14$ from the left-hand side. We do this by adding $14$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-14 & =6 \\ 2x-14+14 & =6+14 \\ 2x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =20 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{20}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & =10 \\ x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?
If 7(x−2)=3(x+2)+2x, then x=
10
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we expand the parentheses on both sides:

7(x−2)=3(x+2)+2x7⋅x−7⋅2=3⋅x+3⋅2+2x7x−14=3x+6+2x7x−14=6+3x+2x7x−14=6+5x

Now, we must bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side.

Notice that we have 7x on the left-hand side and 5x on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side.

The first step is to remove the 5x from the right-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting 5x from both sides:

7x−14=6+5x7x−14−5x=6+5x−5x2x−14=6

Next, we remove the −14 from the left-hand side. We do this by adding 14 to both sides:

2x−14=62x−14+14=6+142x=20

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by 2:

2x=202x2=2022x2=10x=10

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: $\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{4}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=4{x}^{7}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 4{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{8}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})(\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})(\frac{4}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-2\int {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-\frac{{x}^{8}}{4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=6\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,v=\int 6\sqrt{x}\,dx=4{x}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}6\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{e}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})(4{x}^{3/2}){|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}(4{x}^{3/2})(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[4{e}^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-4(1)^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡((1)^{2})]-8{\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{e}^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-\frac{16{x}^{3/2}}{3}{|}_{1}^{{e}^{4}} \\  & =8{e}^{3/2}-(\frac{16{e}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(24{e}^{3/2}-16{e}^{3/2}+16) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(8{e}^{3/2}+16) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}({e}^{3/2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=2{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int 2{x}^{2}\,dx=\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\frac{2({e}^{2})^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2(1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)}{3}]-\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{6}}{3}-(\frac{2{e}^{6}}{9}-\frac{2}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(12{e}^{6}-2{e}^{6}+2) \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(5{e}^{6}+1).\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{-2} & \,⟹\,v=\int {x}^{-2}\,dx=-{x}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{x}^{-2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(-{x}^{-1}){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}(-{x}^{-1})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{{e}^{2}}-(-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)}{1})]+{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})}{{e}^{2}}+(-{x}^{-1}){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{{e}^{2}}+(-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}+1) \\  & =1-\frac{3}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{3}{{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Calculate $\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\cdot (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(3x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(5x))(2\sqrt{x})-\int (2\sqrt{x})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}{log}_{2}⁡(5x)-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{4\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\cdot (3{x}^{3})-\int \frac{3{x}^{3}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {x}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Calculate $\int 25{x}^{4}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{5}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\ {v}^{′}=25{x}^{4}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 25{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x=5{x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 25{x}^{4}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡(5x)\cdot (5{x}^{5})-\int \frac{5{x}^{5}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{x}^{5}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int 5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{x}^{5}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot {x}^{5}+C \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{5}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \,\text{d}x=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\,{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use a substitution $x+1=u,$ thus $x=u-1$ and $\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{u-1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \,\text{d}u+\int \frac{\text{d}u}{u} \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-u+\operatorname{ln}⁡u+D \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(x+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+D \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=D-1$ is an integral constant.

questions.name: Question 12
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1/2}^{e/2}-{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,(x){|}_{1/2}^{e/2}-{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}x(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2})\,(\frac{e}{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})\,(\frac{1}{2})]-{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{e}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-x{|}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}e-\frac{1}{2}e+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{ln}⁡2x\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{ln}⁡2x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \,\text{d}x=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\,{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-x+C \\  & =x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

questions.name: Question 14
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}x(\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{log}_{5}⁡(({e}^{3})^{3})\,({e}^{3})-{log}_{5}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3}{log}_{5}⁡({e}^{9})-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & ={e}^{3}\cdot \frac{9}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{6{e}^{3}+3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}x(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{3})^{2})\,({e}^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})\,(1)]-2{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-2x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =6{e}^{3}-2({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =4{e}^{3}+2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing a Natural Logarithm
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{1}^{e} 4x\ln\left(x^3\right) \textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and $v',$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}=\frac{3}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{e}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot (2{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}(2{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{3}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2{(e)}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3})-2{(1)}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})]-6{\int }_{1}^{e}x\text{d}x \\  & =6{e}^{2}-6(\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3{x}^{2}{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3({e}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{\log_4{x}}{x^3} \,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{4}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{4}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{4}⁡x(-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,{log}_{4}⁡x+\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})+C \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =-\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula $\log_4{x}=\dfrac{\ln{x}}{\ln{4}}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing a Single Logarithmic Factor
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \ln{x}\,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
At first, it may not look like we have two factors. Actually, we do, but one of them is implicit. The trick is to write the integral as

$$
\int \ln{x}\,\textrm{d}x = \int \ln{x} \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Using this trick, we can now use integration by parts. We let

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the by-parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+C \\  & =x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we want to evaluate the integral

$$
\int x\ln{x}\, \textrm{d}x \,.
$$

The method of integration by parts can help us solve this problem. Let's remind ourselves of the "by-parts" formula,

$$
\int u v' \textrm{d}x = uv - \int v u'\textrm{d}x.
$$

We usually let $u = x,$ but that would leave us with $v' = \ln(x)$ which is hard to integrate. So instead, we're going to choose our $u$ and $v'$ slightly differently, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now the formula of integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int {{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{u}\cdot {{x}_{⏟}}_{{v}^{′}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}-\int \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{2}\int x\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

When we apply integration by parts to integrals containing logarithmic functions, we should *always* identify the logarithmic function with $u,$ not with $v'.$

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$

We define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{4}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{4}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{4}⁡x(-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,{log}_{4}⁡x+\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})+C \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =-\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C,\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

Calculate ∫xlog2⁡(3x)dx.

a
x4ln⁡2(2ln⁡(3x)+1)+C
b
x22ln⁡2(ln⁡(3x)−1)+C
c
x24ln⁡2(2ln⁡(3x)−1)+C
d
x22ln⁡2(ln⁡(3x)+2)+C
e
x22ln⁡2(xln⁡(3x)−2)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(3x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=x⟹v=∫xdx=x22

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫xlog2⁡(3x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=log2⁡(3x)⋅(x22)−∫(x22)(1xln⁡2)dx=x2log2⁡(3x)2−12ln⁡2∫xdx=x2ln⁡(3x)2ln⁡2−x24ln⁡2+C=x24ln⁡2(2ln⁡(3x)−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.
question.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Question 7
?

Calculate ∫x2log2⁡(x)dx.

a
x29ln⁡2(ln⁡x−3)+C
b
x29ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C
c
x33ln⁡2(ln⁡x−1)+C
d
x39ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C
e
x33ln⁡2(ln⁡x−3)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=x2⟹v=∫x2dx=x33

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫x2log2⁡(x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(x))(x33)−∫(x33)(1xln⁡2)dx=x3log2⁡(x)3−13ln⁡2∫x2dx=x3ln⁡x3ln⁡2−x39ln⁡2+C=x39ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(5x))(2\sqrt{x})-\int (2\sqrt{x})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}{log}_{2}⁡(5x)-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{4\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Calculate ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx.

a
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
b
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C
c
4xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+1)+C
d
xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+2)+C
e
4xln⁡2(2ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(5x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=1x⟹v=∫1xdx=2x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(5x))(2x)−∫(2x)(1xln⁡2)dx=2xlog2⁡(5x)−2ln⁡2∫1xdx=2xln⁡(5x)ln⁡2−4xln⁡2+C=2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\cdot (3{x}^{3})-\int \frac{3{x}^{3}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {x}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Calculate ∫9x2log3⁡(2x)dx.

a
x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
b
3x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
c
9x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
d
x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)+1)+C
e
3x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)+1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log3⁡(2x)⟹u′=1xln⁡3v′=9x2⟹v=∫9x2dx=3x3

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫9x2log3⁡(2x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=log3⁡(2x)⋅(3x3)−∫3x3xln⁡3dx=3x3log3⁡(2x)−1ln⁡3∫3x2dx=3x3log3⁡(2x)−1ln⁡3⋅x3+C=3x3ln⁡(2x)ln⁡3−x3ln⁡3+C=x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log3⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡3.

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{5}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\ {v}^{′}=25{x}^{4}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 25{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x=5{x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 25{x}^{4}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡(5x)\cdot (5{x}^{5})-\int \frac{5{x}^{5}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{x}^{5}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int 5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{x}^{5}{log}_{5}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot {x}^{5}+C \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{5}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Calculate ∫25x4log5⁡(5x)dx.

a
25x5ln⁡5(ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
b
x5ln⁡5(5ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
c
x5ln⁡5(ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
d
5x5ln⁡5(ln⁡(5x)+1)+C
e
5x5ln⁡5(5ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log5⁡(5x)⟹u′=1xln⁡5v′=25x4⟹v=∫25x4dx=5x5

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫25x4log5⁡(5x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=log5⁡(5x)⋅(5x5)−∫5x5xln⁡5dx=5x5log5⁡(5x)−1ln⁡5∫5x4dx=5x5log5⁡(5x)−1ln⁡5⋅x5+C=5x5ln⁡(5x)ln⁡5−x5ln⁡5+C=x5ln⁡5(5ln⁡(5x)−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log5⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡5.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
observed_steps.worked_solution:
At first, it may not look like we have two factors. Actually, we do, but one of them is implicit. The trick is to write the integral as

$$
\int \ln{x}\,\textrm{d}x = \int \ln{x} \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Using this trick, we can now use integration by parts. We let

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the by-parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+C \\  & =x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \,\text{d}x=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\,{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use a substitution $x+1=u,$ thus $x=u-1$ and $\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{u-1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \,\text{d}u+\int \frac{\text{d}u}{u} \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-u+\operatorname{ln}⁡u+D \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(x+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+D \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=D-1$ is an integral constant.

Question 11
?

∫ln⁡(x+1)dx=

a
xln⁡(x+1)−x+C
b
xx+1−xln⁡x+C
c
xln⁡(x+1)+ln⁡(x+1)−x+C
d
xln⁡x+ln⁡(x+1)+C
e
xln⁡(x+1)+ln⁡x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write the integral as ∫ln⁡(x+1)dx=∫ln⁡(x+1)⋅1⋅dx.

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=ln⁡(x+1)⟹u′=1x+1v′=1⟹v=∫dx=x

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫ln⁡(x+1)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=ln⁡(x+1)⋅x−∫x⋅1x+1dx=xln⁡(x+1)−∫xx+1dx.

Now, we use a substitution x+1=u, thus x=u−1 and dx=du. Hence, ∫ln⁡(x+1)dx=xln⁡(x+1)−∫xx+1dx=xln⁡(x+1)−∫u−1udu=xln⁡(x+1)−∫du+∫duu=xln⁡(x+1)−u+ln⁡u+D=xln⁡(x+1)−(x+1)+ln⁡(x+1)+D=xln⁡(x+1)+ln⁡(x+1)−x+C, where C=D−1 is an integral constant.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1/2}^{e/2}-{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,(x){|}_{1/2}^{e/2}-{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}x(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2})\,(\frac{e}{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})\,(\frac{1}{2})]-{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{e}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-x{|}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}e-\frac{1}{2}e+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing a Single Logarithmic Factor
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{ln}⁡2x\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{ln}⁡2x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \,\text{d}x=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\,{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-x+C \\  & =x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

question.problem: $\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{4}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=4{x}^{7}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 4{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{8}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})(\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})(\frac{4}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-2\int {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-\frac{{x}^{8}}{4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Question 1
?

∫4x7ln⁡x4dx=

a
x8ln⁡x432−x832+C
b
x8ln⁡x42−x83+C
c
x8ln⁡x42−x84+C
d
x8ln⁡x44−x832+C
e
x8ln⁡x44−x816+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=ln⁡(x4)⟹u′=4xv′=4x7⟹v=∫4x7dx=x82

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫4x7ln⁡(x4)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=ln⁡(x4)(x82)−∫(x82)(4x)dx=x8ln⁡(x4)2−2∫x7dx=x8ln⁡(x4)2−x84+C, where C is an integral constant.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing a Natural Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{4}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=4{x}^{7}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 4{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{8}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})(\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})(\frac{4}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-2\int {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-\frac{{x}^{8}}{4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

feedback.problem: $\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{4}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=4{x}^{7}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 4{x}^{7}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{8}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})(\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{8}}{2})(\frac{4}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-2\int {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})}{2}-\frac{{x}^{8}}{4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=6\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,v=\int 6\sqrt{x}\,dx=4{x}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Calculate $\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\cdot (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(3x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Calculate ∫xlog2⁡(3x)dx.

a
x4ln⁡2(2ln⁡(3x)+1)+C
b
x22ln⁡2(ln⁡(3x)−1)+C
c
x24ln⁡2(2ln⁡(3x)−1)+C
d
x22ln⁡2(ln⁡(3x)+2)+C
e
x22ln⁡2(xln⁡(3x)−2)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(3x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=x⟹v=∫xdx=x22

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫xlog2⁡(3x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=log2⁡(3x)⋅(x22)−∫(x22)(1xln⁡2)dx=x2log2⁡(3x)2−12ln⁡2∫xdx=x2ln⁡(3x)2ln⁡2−x24ln⁡2+C=x24ln⁡2(2ln⁡(3x)−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\cdot (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(3x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

feedback.problem: Calculate $\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(3x)\cdot (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(3x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Calculate ∫x2log2⁡(x)dx.

a
x29ln⁡2(ln⁡x−3)+C
b
x29ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C
c
x33ln⁡2(ln⁡x−1)+C
d
x39ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C
e
x33ln⁡2(ln⁡x−3)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=x2⟹v=∫x2dx=x33

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫x2log2⁡(x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(x))(x33)−∫(x33)(1xln⁡2)dx=x3log2⁡(x)3−13ln⁡2∫x2dx=x3ln⁡x3ln⁡2−x39ln⁡2+C=x39ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Calculate ∫x2log2⁡(x)dx.

a
x29ln⁡2(ln⁡x−3)+C
b
x29ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C
c
x33ln⁡2(ln⁡x−1)+C
d
x39ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C
e
x33ln⁡2(ln⁡x−3)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=x2⟹v=∫x2dx=x33

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫x2log2⁡(x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(x))(x33)−∫(x33)(1xln⁡2)dx=x3log2⁡(x)3−13ln⁡2∫x2dx=x3ln⁡x3ln⁡2−x39ln⁡2+C=x39ln⁡2(3ln⁡x−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.
question.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm

solution.reasoning: Change of base gives log_2(x)=\ln x/\ln 2. Integration by parts with u=\ln x and v=x^3/3 yields x^3\ln x/(3\ln 2)-x^3/(9\ln 2)+C, matching option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked solution concerns a different integral.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(5x))(2\sqrt{x})-\int (2\sqrt{x})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}{log}_{2}⁡(5x)-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{4\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Calculate ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx.

a
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
b
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C
c
4xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+1)+C
d
xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+2)+C
e
4xln⁡2(2ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(5x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=1x⟹v=∫1xdx=2x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(5x))(2x)−∫(2x)(1xln⁡2)dx=2xlog2⁡(5x)−2ln⁡2∫1xdx=2xln⁡(5x)ln⁡2−4xln⁡2+C=2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

last_observation.name: Question 8
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(5x))(2\sqrt{x})-\int (2\sqrt{x})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}{log}_{2}⁡(5x)-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{4\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Calculate ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx.

a
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
b
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C
c
4xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+1)+C
d
xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+2)+C
e
4xln⁡2(2ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(5x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=1x⟹v=∫1xdx=2x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(5x))(2x)−∫(2x)(1xln⁡2)dx=2xlog2⁡(5x)−2ln⁡2∫1xdx=2xln⁡(5x)ln⁡2−4xln⁡2+C=2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.
question.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm

solution.reasoning: Using change of base and integration by parts with u=\ln(5x), du=dx/x, and v=2\sqrt{x}, the integral equals [2\sqrt{x}\ln(5x)-4\sqrt{x}]/\ln 2+C, matching option b. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different integral.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡(5x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡(5x)}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡(5x))(2\sqrt{x})-\int (2\sqrt{x})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}{log}_{2}⁡(5x)-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{4\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)-2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Question 8
?

Calculate ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx.

a
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
b
2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C
c
4xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+1)+C
d
xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)+2)+C
e
4xln⁡2(2ln⁡(5x)−1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log2⁡(5x)⟹u′=1xln⁡2v′=1x⟹v=∫1xdx=2x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫log2⁡(5x)xdx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=(log2⁡(5x))(2x)−∫(2x)(1xln⁡2)dx=2xlog2⁡(5x)−2ln⁡2∫1xdx=2xln⁡(5x)ln⁡2−4xln⁡2+C=2xln⁡2(ln⁡(5x)−2)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Calculate $\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\cdot (3{x}^{3})-\int \frac{3{x}^{3}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {x}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Calculate ∫9x2log3⁡(2x)dx.

a
x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
b
3x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
c
9x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
d
x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)+1)+C
e
3x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)+1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log3⁡(2x)⟹u′=1xln⁡3v′=9x2⟹v=∫9x2dx=3x3

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫9x2log3⁡(2x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=log3⁡(2x)⋅(3x3)−∫3x3xln⁡3dx=3x3log3⁡(2x)−1ln⁡3∫3x2dx=3x3log3⁡(2x)−1ln⁡3⋅x3+C=3x3ln⁡(2x)ln⁡3−x3ln⁡3+C=x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log3⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡3.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\cdot (3{x}^{3})-\int \frac{3{x}^{3}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {x}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Question 9
?

Calculate ∫9x2log3⁡(2x)dx.

a
x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
b
3x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
c
9x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)−1)+C
d
x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)+1)+C
e
3x3ln⁡3(ln⁡(2x)+1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining u and v′, as follows:

u=log3⁡(2x)⟹u′=1xln⁡3v′=9x2⟹v=∫9x2dx=3x3

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫9x2log3⁡(2x)dx=∫uv′dx=uv−∫vu′dx=log3⁡(2x)⋅(3x3)−∫3x3xln⁡3dx=3x3log3⁡(2x)−1ln⁡3∫3x2dx=3x3log3⁡(2x)−1ln⁡3⋅x3+C=3x3ln⁡(2x)ln⁡3−x3ln⁡3+C=x3ln⁡3(3ln⁡(2x)−1)+C, where C is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log3⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡3.

solution.reasoning: Change of base gives \log_3(2x)=\ln(2x)/\ln 3. Integration by parts with u=\ln(2x) and v=3x^3 yields [3x^3\ln(2x)-x^3]/\ln 3+C, matching option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked solution concerns a different integral.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\cdot (3{x}^{3})-\int \frac{3{x}^{3}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {x}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$
