feedback.worked_solution:
The infimum of $A$ is the greatest lower bound of $A.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=2-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14162617/assets/72fa47f25042b5187a87262b23e0976429909011b1516bc6018e70cd4f881f11.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is increasing and converges to $5.$ The minimum of $A$ is 

$$
min(A)={a}_{1}=2-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}=\frac{5}{3}.
$$

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $x\le {a}_{1}$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $x>{a}_{1}$ cannot be a lower bound because ${a}_{1},$ an element of $A,$ is smaller than $x.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{3}]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
inf(A)=max(-\infty ,\frac{5}{3}]=\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Notice that $\frac{5}{3}$ is the minimum of $A.$ Therefore, we conclude that

$$
inf(A)=\frac{5}{3}\in A.
$$

question.worked_solution:
The infimum of a function is the infimum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=(-\infty ,3).$

To find the infimum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, $A$ has no lower bounds. We can always find an element $x$ such that $f(x)$ is smaller than $y$ for any $y.$ 

Therefore, ${inf}_{x\in R}f(x)$ $=-\infty .$

question.html:
Question 16
?
What is the infimum of the function y=f(x) shown above?infx∈Rf(x)
=−∞
=−1
=−∞
=0
=2
=3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The infimum of a function is the infimum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of f is A=(−∞,3).

To find the infimum of a set A, we must find the set containing all lower bounds of A (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, A has no lower bounds. We can always find an element x such that f(x) is smaller than y for any y.

Therefore, infx∈Rf(x) =−∞.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14162617/assets/372aa80e15465694347dce5325537a10be1217e83050d609dfeec0347bad1116.png)

What is the infimum of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

${inf}_{x\in R}f(x)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The infimum of a function is the infimum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=[-2,2].$

To find the infimum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y\le -2$ is a lower bound of $A,$

- any number $y>-2$ is **not** a lower bound of $A$ because $-2,$ an element of $A,$ is smaller than $y.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-2]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and

$$
{inf}_{x\in R}f(x)=inf(A)=max(-\infty ,-2]=-2.
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14162617/assets/0d745d274250c84f6701ff22d17d0c6506a9f03f4a1a461e09f609a0ea11d99b.png)

What is the supremum of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

${sup}_{x\in R}f(x)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The supremum of a function is the supremum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=[-2,1).$

To find the supremum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y\ge 1$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $y<1$ is **not** an upper bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $A$ that is greater than $y$ for any $y<1.$

Therefore, $[1,\infty )$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and

$$
{sup}_{x\in R}f(x)=sup(A)=min[1,\infty )=1.
$$

Therefore, ${sup}_{x\ge -1}f(x)$ $=+\infty .$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: A medical doctor records the temperature of ${100}^{∘}\text{F}$ using a thermometer. After the measurement is taken, the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, $T$ is measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and $t>0$ is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is ${64}^{∘}\text{F},$ which differential equation could be used to model the thermometer reading? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={64}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-64).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Modeling Inhibited Decay
questions.raw_html:
1.Modeling Inhibited Decay?

A medical doctor records the temperature of 100∘F using a thermometer. After the measurement is taken, the temperature reading T(t) of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, T is measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and t>0 is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is 64∘F, which differential equation could be used to model the thermometer reading? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the body in degrees Celsius, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${21}^{∘}\text{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={21}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-21).
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of a fresh-baked cake can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.09(T-70)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the cake is ${340}^{∘}F,$ calculate the temperature of the cake after $8$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fresh-baked cake is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.09(T-70).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-70} & =-0.09\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-70} & =-\int 0.09\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-70| & =-0.09t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-70>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-70 & ={e}^{-0.09t+C} \\ T-70 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T-70 & =K{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T & =70+K{e}^{-0.09t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the cake was ${340}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=340,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}340 & =70+K{e}^{0} \\ 340 & =70+K \\ K & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=70+270{e}^{-0.09t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the cake after $t=8$ minutes is

$$
T(8)=70+270{e}^{-0.09\cdot 8}≈{201}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${60}^{∘}C.$ After $10$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${52}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${40}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${52}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=52,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =28+32{e}^{-10k} \\ 24 & =32{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${40}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =40 \\ 28+32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =40 \\ 32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =12 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{3}{8} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${40}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8})}{-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}≈34\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of an exhaust pipe of a motorcycle can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe is ${140}^{∘}F,$ calculate its temperature after $3$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-74} & =-0.08\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-74} & =-\int 0.08\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-74| & =-0.08t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-74>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.08t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.08t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${140}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=140,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}140 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 140 & =74+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+66{e}^{-0.08t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=74+66{e}^{-0.08\cdot 3}≈{126}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={64}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-64).
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let T(t) be the temperature of the body in degrees Celsius, and let t>0 be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is 21∘C, which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
T′(t)=−kT(T−21)
b
T′(t)=−k(T−21)
c
T′(t)=k(T+21)
d
T′(t)=−k(T+21)
e
T′(t)=kT(T−21)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=21∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−21).

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fresh-baked cake is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.09(T-70).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-70} & =-0.09\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-70} & =-\int 0.09\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-70| & =-0.09t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-70>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-70 & ={e}^{-0.09t+C} \\ T-70 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T-70 & =K{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T & =70+K{e}^{-0.09t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the cake was ${340}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=340,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}340 & =70+K{e}^{0} \\ 340 & =70+K \\ K & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=70+270{e}^{-0.09t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the cake after $t=8$ minutes is

$$
T(8)=70+270{e}^{-0.09\cdot 8}≈{201}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${52}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=52,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =28+32{e}^{-10k} \\ 24 & =32{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${40}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =40 \\ 28+32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =40 \\ 32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =12 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{3}{8} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${40}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8})}{-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}≈34\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${60}^{∘}C.$ After $10$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${52}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${40}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
question.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${52}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=52,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =28+32{e}^{-10k} \\ 24 & =32{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${40}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =40 \\ 28+32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =40 \\ 32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =12 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{3}{8} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${40}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8})}{-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}≈34\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of 60∘C. After 10 minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of 52∘C. Hint: You may assume that the temperature T(t) of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where T is measured in degrees Celsius and t>0 is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.

a

b

c

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=28∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−28).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

dTT−28=−kdt∫dTT−28=−k∫dtln⁡|T−28|=−kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have T−28>0 for all t>0. Next, we solve for T(t), as follows:

T−28=e−kt+CT−28=eCe−ktT−28=Ke−ktT=28+Ke−kt

Note that K=eC is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial temperature reading was 60∘C. So, we apply the initial condition T(0)=60, and solve for K:

60=28+Ke060=28+KK=32

Therefore, we have the following expression for T(t):

T(t)=28+32e−kt

We're also told that, after 10 minutes, the thermometer reading is 52∘C. So, applying the condition T(10)=52, we can solve for k:

52=28+32e−10k24=32e−10k34=e−10kln⁡(34)=−10kk=−110ln⁡(34)

Finally, let t1 be the time when the temperature of the tea is 40∘C. Then, we have

T(t1)=4028+32e−kt1=4032e−kt1=12e−kt1=38−kt1=ln⁡(38)t1=−1kln⁡(38).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of 40∘C after

t1=−ln⁡(38)−110ln⁡(34)≈34min,

rounded to the nearest minute.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-74} & =-0.08\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-74} & =-\int 0.08\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-74| & =-0.08t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-74>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.08t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.08t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${140}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=140,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}140 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 140 & =74+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+66{e}^{-0.08t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=74+66{e}^{-0.08\cdot 3}≈{126}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.html:
Question 1
?

A medical doctor records the temperature of 100∘F using a thermometer. After the measurement is taken, the temperature reading T(t) of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, T is measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and t>0 is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is 64∘F, which differential equation could be used to model the thermometer reading? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
dTdt=−k(T−100)
b
dTdt=−k(T−164)
c
dTdt=−64(T−100)
d
dTdt=−k(T−64)
e
dTdt=−100(T−64)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=64∘F, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−64).

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={64}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-64).
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: A medical doctor records the temperature of ${100}^{∘}\text{F}$ using a thermometer. After the measurement is taken, the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, $T$ is measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and $t>0$ is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is ${64}^{∘}\text{F},$ which differential equation could be used to model the thermometer reading? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.worked_solution:

question.html:
Question 1
?

A medical doctor records the temperature of 100∘F using a thermometer. After the measurement is taken, the temperature reading T(t) of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, T is measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and t>0 is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is 64∘F, which differential equation could be used to model the thermometer reading? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
dTdt=−k(T−100)
b
dTdt=−k(T−164)
c
dTdt=−64(T−100)
d
dTdt=−k(T−64)
e
dTdt=−100(T−64)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=64∘F, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−64).

solution.reasoning: Newton's law of cooling gives dT/dt = -k(T-64), since the ambient temperature is 64°F. For T>64 and k>0, the derivative is negative, as required. The initial reading supplies T(0)=100, not the equilibrium temperature. Option d is mathematically correct; no Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was captured.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: A medical doctor records the temperature of ${100}^{∘}\text{F}$ using a thermometer. After the measurement is taken, the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, $T$ is measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and $t>0$ is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is ${64}^{∘}\text{F},$ which differential equation could be used to model the thermometer reading? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
feedback.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={64}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-64).
$$

question.problem: The rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the body in degrees Celsius, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${21}^{∘}\text{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={21}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-21).
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let T(t) be the temperature of the body in degrees Celsius, and let t>0 be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is 21∘C, which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
T′(t)=−kT(T−21)
b
T′(t)=−k(T−21)
c
T′(t)=k(T+21)
d
T′(t)=−k(T+21)
e
T′(t)=kT(T−21)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=21∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−21).

question.html:
Question 2
?

The rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let T(t) be the temperature of the body in degrees Celsius, and let t>0 be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is 21∘C, which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
T′(t)=−kT(T−21)
b
T′(t)=−k(T−21)
c
T′(t)=k(T+21)
d
T′(t)=−k(T+21)
e
T′(t)=kT(T−21)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=21∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−21).

solution.reasoning: Newton's law of cooling gives T′(t)=-k(T-21): the rate is proportional to the temperature difference, with a negative sign so a body above 21°C cools toward 21°C. Thus option b is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grading evidence was captured.

Question 2
?

The rate at which a body cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let T(t) be the temperature of the body in degrees Celsius, and let t>0 be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is 21∘C, which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
T′(t)=−kT(T−21)
b
T′(t)=−k(T−21)
c
T′(t)=k(T+21)
d
T′(t)=−k(T+21)
e
T′(t)=kT(T−21)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=21∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−21).

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of a fresh-baked cake can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.09(T-70)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the cake is ${340}^{∘}F,$ calculate the temperature of the cake after $8$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
question.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fresh-baked cake is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.09(T-70).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-70} & =-0.09\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-70} & =-\int 0.09\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-70| & =-0.09t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-70>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-70 & ={e}^{-0.09t+C} \\ T-70 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T-70 & =K{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T & =70+K{e}^{-0.09t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the cake was ${340}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=340,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}340 & =70+K{e}^{0} \\ 340 & =70+K \\ K & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=70+270{e}^{-0.09t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the cake after $t=8$ minutes is

$$
T(8)=70+270{e}^{-0.09\cdot 8}≈{201}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

a

b
198∘F
c

194∘F
e
223∘F

dTT−70=−0.09dt∫dTT−70=−∫0.09dtln⁡|T−70|=−0.09t+C

340=70+Ke0340=70+KK=270

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fresh-baked cake is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.09(T-70).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-70} & =-0.09\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-70} & =-\int 0.09\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-70| & =-0.09t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-70>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-70 & ={e}^{-0.09t+C} \\ T-70 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T-70 & =K{e}^{-0.09t} \\ T & =70+K{e}^{-0.09t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the cake was ${340}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=340,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}340 & =70+K{e}^{0} \\ 340 & =70+K \\ K & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=70+270{e}^{-0.09t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the cake after $t=8$ minutes is

$$
T(8)=70+270{e}^{-0.09\cdot 8}≈{201}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${60}^{∘}C.$ After $10$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${52}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${40}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
question.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${52}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=52,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =28+32{e}^{-10k} \\ 24 & =32{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of 60∘C. After 10 minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of 52∘C. To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to 40∘C if the temperature in the room is 28∘C?

Hint: You may assume that the temperature T(t) of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where T is measured in degrees Celsius and t>0 is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.

a
23min
b
31min
c
28min
d
34min
e
45min
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=28∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−28).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

dTT−28=−kdt∫dTT−28=−k∫dtln⁡|T−28|=−kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have T−28>0 for all t>0. Next, we solve for T(t), as follows:

T−28=e−kt+CT−28=eCe−ktT−28=Ke−ktT=28+Ke−kt

Note that K=eC is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial temperature reading was 60∘C. So, we apply the initial condition T(0)=60, and solve for K:

60=28+Ke060=28+KK=32

Therefore, we have the following expression for T(t):

T(t)=28+32e−kt

We're also told that, after 10 minutes, the thermometer reading is 52∘C. So, applying the condition T(10)=52, we can solve for k:

52=28+32e−10k24=32e−10k34=e−10kln⁡(34)=−10kk=−110ln⁡(34)

Finally, let t1 be the time when the temperature of the tea is 40∘C. Then, we have

T(t1)=4028+32e−kt1=4032e−kt1=12e−kt1=38−kt1=ln⁡(38)t1=−1kln⁡(38).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of 40∘C after

t1=−ln⁡(38)−110ln⁡(34)≈34min,

rounded to the nearest minute.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${60}^{∘}C.$ After $10$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${52}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${40}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
feedback.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${52}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=52,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =28+32{e}^{-10k} \\ 24 & =32{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${40}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =40 \\ 28+32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =40 \\ 32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =12 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{3}{8} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${40}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8})}{-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}≈34\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of an exhaust pipe of a motorcycle can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe is ${140}^{∘}F,$ calculate its temperature after $3$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
question.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-74} & =-0.08\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-74} & =-\int 0.08\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-74| & =-0.08t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-74>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.08t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.08t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${140}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=140,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}140 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 140 & =74+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+66{e}^{-0.08t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=74+66{e}^{-0.08\cdot 3}≈{126}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-74).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-74} & =-0.08\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-74} & =-\int 0.08\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-74| & =-0.08t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-74>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-74 & ={e}^{-0.08t+C} \\ T-74 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T-74 & =K{e}^{-0.08t} \\ T & =74+K{e}^{-0.08t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was ${140}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=140,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}140 & =74+K{e}^{0} \\ 140 & =74+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=74+66{e}^{-0.08t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after $t=3$ minutes is

$$
T(3)=74+66{e}^{-0.08\cdot 3}≈{126}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.html:
Question 5
?

The temperature T(t), in degrees Fahrenheit, of an exhaust pipe of a motorcycle can be modeled by the differential equation

dTdt=−0.08(T−74) where t>0 is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe is 140∘F, calculate its temperature after 3 minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.

a
126∘F
b
98∘F
c
92∘F
d
112∘F
e
134∘F
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We're told that the temperature of the exhaust pipe of a motorcycle is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

dTdt=−0.08(T−74).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

dTT−74=−0.08dt∫dTT−74=−∫0.08dtln⁡|T−74|=−0.08t+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have T−74>0 for all t>0. Next, we solve for T(t), as follows:

T−74=e−0.08t+CT−74=eCe−0.08tT−74=Ke−0.08tT=74+Ke−0.08t

Note that K=eC is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial temperature of the exhaust pipe was 140∘F. So, we apply the initial condition T(0)=140, and solve for K:

140=74+Ke0140=74+KK=66

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

T(t)=74+66e−0.08t.

Finally, the temperature of the exhaust pipe after t=3 minutes is T(3)=74+66e−0.08⋅3≈126∘F, rounded to the nearest integer.

solution.reasoning: The solution is T(t)=74+Ce^{-0.08t}. Using T(0)=140 gives C=66, so T(3)=74+66e^{-0.24}≈125.917°F. Rounded to the nearest integer, this is 126°F, option a. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was captured.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Evaluate $Γ(5).$
questions.worked_solution:
For any natural number $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
Γ(n)=(n-1)!.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Γ(5)=4!=24.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Evaluate $\sqrt{\pi }\,Γ(\frac{7}{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),\,Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi }
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\pi }\,Γ(\frac{7}{2}) & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}Γ(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi } \\  & =\frac{15\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),\,Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi }
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\pi }\,Γ(\frac{7}{2}) & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}Γ(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi } \\  & =\frac{15\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),\,Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi }
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi },
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(\frac{5}{2})=\frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi }=\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
2\,Γ(\frac{5}{2})+Γ(\frac{3}{2})=2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi }=2\sqrt{\pi }.
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Evaluate $\sqrt{\pi }\,Γ(\frac{7}{2}).$
question.worked_solution:
To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),\,Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi }
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\pi }\,Γ(\frac{7}{2}) & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}Γ(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\pi }\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi } \\  & =\frac{15\pi }{8}\end{aligned}

To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),Γ(12)=π

So, we have the following:

πΓ(72)=π⋅52Γ(52)=π⋅52⋅32Γ(32)=π⋅52⋅32⋅12Γ(12)=π⋅52⋅32⋅12π=15π8

Question 5
?

2Γ(52)+Γ(32)=

a
2π
b
8π
c
3π
d
4π
e
6π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),Γ(12)=π

So, we have the following:

Γ(32)=12Γ(12)=12π,

Γ(52)=32Γ(32)=32⋅12π=34π

Therefore,

2Γ(52)+Γ(32)=2⋅34π+12π=2π.

questions.problem:
Expressed as a polynomial in terms of $x,$ the length of Paul's plot of land is{{field-1}}
yards.
questions.worked_solution:
The width of the plot is $x+5$ yards, and its area is $3{x}^{2}+15x$ square yards. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(3{x}^{2},15x)=3x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+15x & = \\ (3x\cdot x)+(3x\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x\cdot x)+(3x\cdot 5) & = \\ 3x(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $3x$ yards.

Paul's neighbor to the south, Karol, has a land plot of area ${x}^{2}+2x-8$ square yards, as shown in the picture. Given that the length of Karol's plot of land is $x+4$ yards, what is the width of the plot in terms of $x?$

Karol's plot width is
{{field-1}}
yards.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the required width, we need to factor the expression ${x}^{2}+2x-8.$

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-8).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-8) \\ (-1) & \times 8 \\ 2 & \times (-4) \\ (-2) & \times 4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-8) & =-7 & \times  \\ -1+8 & =7 & \times  \\ 2+(-4) & =-2 & \times  \\ -2+4 & =2 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $2x=4x-2x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-8 & ={x}^{2}+4x-2x-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x-2x-8 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+4x)+(-2x-8) & = \\ x(x+4)-2(x+4) & = \\ (x-2)(x+4)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the width must be $x-2$ yards.

Let $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. Then, according to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$

questions.problem:
Paul purchased his land for $400$ thousand dollars. The value of the land increases by $10%$ each year. How much will Paul's plot be worth after $5$ years? Round your answer to the nearest thousand dollars.

After $5$ years, the land will be worth approximately 
{{field-1}}
 thousand dollars.
questions.worked_solution:
The land initially costs $400$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $10%$ per year.

$10%$ as a decimal is $0.1.$ Therefore, an increase of $10%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.1=1.1.
$$

Therefore, we have:

* After $1$ year, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)$ thousand dollars

* After $2$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{2}$ thousand dollars

* After $3$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{3}$ thousand dollars

* After $4$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{4}$ thousand dollars

* After $5$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{5}$ thousand dollars 

Evaluating the expression for the value after $5$ years, we get the following:

$$
400\cdot (1.1)^{5}=644.204≈644,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $5$ years, the land will be worth approximately $644$ thousand dollars.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The land initially costs $400$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $10%$ per year.

$10%$ as a decimal is $0.1.$ Therefore, an increase of $10%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.1=1.1.
$$

Therefore, we have:

- After $1$ year, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)$ thousand dollars

- After $2$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{2}$ thousand dollars

- After $3$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{3}$ thousand dollars

- After $4$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{4}$ thousand dollars

- After $5$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{5}$ thousand dollars

Evaluating the expression for the value after $5$ years, we get the following:

$$
400\cdot (1.1)^{5}=644.204≈644,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $5$ years, the land will be worth approximately $644$ thousand dollars.

$$

question.problem:
Expressed as a polynomial in terms of $x,$ the length of Paul's plot of land is

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
yards.
question.worked_solution:
The width of the plot is $x+5$ yards, and its area is $3{x}^{2}+15x$ square yards. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(3{x}^{2},15x)=3x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+15x & = \\ (3x\cdot x)+(3x\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x\cdot x)+(3x\cdot 5) & = \\ 3x(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $3x$ yards.

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-8).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-8) \\ (-1) & \times 8 \\ 2 & \times (-4) \\ (-2) & \times 4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-8) & =-7 & \times  \\ -1+8 & =7 & \times  \\ 2+(-4) & =-2 & \times  \\ -2+4 & =2 & ✓\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-8 & ={x}^{2}+4x-2x-8\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x-2x-8 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+4x)+(-2x-8) & = \\ x(x+4)-2(x+4) & = \\ (x-2)(x+4)\end{aligned}

question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have a right triangle with legs $a=24\,\text{yd}$  and $b=18\,\text{yd}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14162885/assets/35dff3715d9e7e06f7c15a3b80c0171820f71e1998695550a7672377d981ee76.png)

Let $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. Then, according to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the values for $a$ and $b$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{{24}^{2}+{18}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{576+324} \\  & =\sqrt{900} \\  & =30\,\text{yd}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Paul purchased his land for $400$ thousand dollars. The value of the land increases by $10%$ each year. How much will Paul's plot be worth after $5$ years? Round your answer to the nearest thousand dollars.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        After $5$ years, the land will be worth approximately 

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
 thousand dollars.
question.worked_solution:
The land initially costs $400$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $10%$ per year.

$10%$ as a decimal is $0.1.$ Therefore, an increase of $10%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.1=1.1.
$$

Therefore, we have:

- After $1$ year, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)$ thousand dollars

- After $2$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{2}$ thousand dollars

- After $3$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{3}$ thousand dollars

- After $4$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{4}$ thousand dollars

- After $5$ years, the value will be $400\cdot (1.1)^{5}$ thousand dollars

Evaluating the expression for the value after $5$ years, we get the following:

$$
400\cdot (1.1)^{5}=644.204≈644,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $5$ years, the land will be worth approximately $644$ thousand dollars.

question.problem:
The value $V(t)$ of Paul's plot of land, in thousands of dollars, can be modeled by the function $V(t)=400\cdot (1.1)^{t},$ where $t$ is the time in years since he bought the land. What is the growth in the value of the plot over the first two years? Round your answer to the nearest thousand dollars.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Paul's land grew in value by

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
 thousand dollars over the first two years.
question.worked_solution:
To find the growth in the value over the first two years, we need to find the value after $2$ years and then subtract the initial cost:

$$
V(2)-V(0)
$$

In the previous part, we were given the initial value of the land:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(0) & =400\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find $V(2),$ the value of the land after $2$ years:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2) & =400\cdot (1.1)^{(2)} \\  & =400\cdot (1.21) \\  & =484\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth in the first two years is

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2)-V(0) & =484-400 \\  & =84.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth in the value of the land over the first two years was $84$ thousand dollars.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=4x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the point $P(0,0)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$  calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =4x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =4-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

1.Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function?

Consider the function f(x)=4x−sin⁡x and the point P(0,0) that lies on y=f(x). Given that f(x) is invertible in the vicinity of P, calculate (f−1)′(0).

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=5,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(5)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(5)=8$ and ${f}^{′}(8)=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(8)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

The figure above shows the graph of a piecewise linear function $y=f(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(1,2)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $(2,1)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2)?$

{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(2,1)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(2)=1.$ 
The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [0,4]$ is $-1$, hence, ${f}^{′}(1)=-1.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is 

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =4x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =4-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
question.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find (g⋅f−1)′(2) of the product of functions, given the following table of values of f(x),f′(x),g(x), and g′(x) at some points.

x f(x) f′(x) g(x) g′(x)
2 0 2 −1 12
1 2 4 3 −1
(g⋅f−1)′(2)=
14​
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the derivative of the inverse f−1(x) is (f−1)′(x)=1f′(f−1(x)).

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function g(x)f−1(x) is (g⋅f−1)′(x)=g′(x)f−1(x)+g(x)f′(f−1(x)).

Substituting x=2, we have (g⋅f−1)′(2)=g′(2)f−1(2)+g(2)f′(f−1(2)).

From the table, we obtain f−1(2)=1, g(2)=−1, g′(2)=12, and f′(1)=4. Therefore,

(g⋅f−1)′(2)=g′(2)f−1(2)+g(2)f′(f−1(2))=12⋅1+(−1)f′(1)=12+(−1)4=12−14=14.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=4x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the point $P(0,0)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$  calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0).$
question.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =4x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =4-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the function f(x)=4x−sin⁡x and the point P(0,0) that lies on y=f(x). Given that f(x) is invertible in the vicinity of P, calculate (f−1)′(0).

a
15
b
−2
c
13
d
−1
e
14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by calculating the derivative of f at the point (0,0). f(x)=4x−sin⁡xf′(x)=4−cos⁡xf′(0)=3

Since (0,0) lies on y=f(x), we know that the corresponding point (0,0) lies on y=f−1(x).

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore, (f−1)′(0)=1f′(f−1(0))=1f′(0)=13.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =4x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =4-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The following table gives the values of functions f(x) and f′(x) at some points. Find (f−1)′(5).

x f(x) f′(x)
3 4 9
5 1 6
8 5 4
a
−6
b
−12
c
14
d
16
e
−14
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The formula for the derivative of the inverse is (f−1)′(x)=1f′(f−1(x)).

Substituting x=5, we have (f−1)′(5)=1f′(f−1(5)).

From the table, we obtain f−1(5)=8 and f′(8)=4. Therefore,

(f−1)′(5)=1f′(f−1(5))=1f′(8)=14.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$

$$

Substituting $x=5,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(5)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(5)=8$ and ${f}^{′}(8)=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(8)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
question.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the value of f−1(2). To do this, we solve the equation f−1(2)=x. For x≠12, this gives f−1(2)=xf(x)=23x+12x−1=23x+12x−1⋅(2x−1)=2⋅(2x−1)3x+1(2x−1)⋅(2x−1)=4x−23x+1=4x−21+2=4x−3xx=3.

Therefore, f−1(2)=3.

Now we calculate f′(3), as follows: f(x)=3x+12x−1f′(x)=−5(2x−1)2f′(3)=−5(2⋅3−1)2=−5(5)2=−15

Question 3
?

Consider the function f(x)=3x+12x−1. Given that y=f(x) is invertible throughout its domain, determine (f−1)′(2).

a
 −15
b
 −59
c
 −13
d
 −5
e
 −95
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To determine (f−1)′(2), we use the following formula: (f−1)′(2)=1f′(f−1(2))

First, we calculate the value of f−1(2). To do this, we solve the equation f−1(2)=x. For x≠12, this gives f−1(2)=xf(x)=23x+12x−1=23x+12x−1⋅(2x−1)=2⋅(2x−1)3x+1(2x−1)⋅(2x−1)=4x−23x+1=4x−21+2=4x−3xx=3.

Therefore, f−1(2)=3.

Now we calculate f′(3), as follows: f(x)=3x+12x−1f′(x)=−5(2x−1)2f′(3)=−5(2⋅3−1)2=−5(5)2=−15

Finally, we get (f−1)′(2)=1f′(f−1(2))=1f′(3)=1(−15)=−5.

solution.reasoning: Solving (3x+1)/(2x-1)=2 gives x=3, so f^{-1}(2)=3. The quotient rule gives f'(x)=-5/(2x-1)^2, hence f'(3)=-1/5. Therefore (f^{-1})'(2)=1/f'(3)=-5, choice d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

The figure above shows the graph of a piecewise linear function $y=f(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(1,2)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $(2,1)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2)?$

$({f}^{-1})^{′}(2)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Since $(2,1)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(2)=1.$ 
The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [0,4]$ is $-1$, hence, ${f}^{′}(1)=-1.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is 

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find (g⋅f−1)′(2) of the product of functions, given the following table of values of f(x),f′(x),g(x), and g′(x) at some points.

x f(x) f′(x) g(x) g′(x)
2 0 2 −1 12
1 2 4 3 −1
(g⋅f−1)′(2)=
14​
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the derivative of the inverse f−1(x) is (f−1)′(x)=1f′(f−1(x)).

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function g(x)f−1(x) is (g⋅f−1)′(x)=g′(x)f−1(x)+g(x)f′(f−1(x)).

Substituting x=2, we have (g⋅f−1)′(2)=g′(2)f−1(2)+g(2)f′(f−1(2)).

From the table, we obtain f−1(2)=1, g(2)=−1, g′(2)=12, and f′(1)=4. Therefore,

(g⋅f−1)′(2)=g′(2)f−1(2)+g(2)f′(f−1(2))=12⋅1+(−1)f′(1)=12+(−1)4=12−14=14.

(g⋅f−1)′(2)=g′(2)f−1(2)+g(2)f′(f−1(2))=12⋅1+(−1)f′(1)=12+(−1)4=12−14=14.

solution.reasoning: Since f(1)=2, f^{-1}(2)=1 and (f^{-1})'(2)=1/f'(1)=1/4. By the product rule, (g·f^{-1})'(2)=g'(2)f^{-1}(2)+g(2)(f^{-1})'(2)=(1/2)(1)+(-1)(1/4)=1/4. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -6 \\ 3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+18) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial  $\,{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8\,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & a & -2 \\ -1 & b & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $(a+b)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{2}I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 12 & -10 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st  and the $2$nd ones). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get  ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $(a+b)^{2}=(0+1)^{2}=1.$
