questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/d963d5620df91a05c8371ef09beeb84546c5f5a8cda047f2c2c3b9933f3d5c01.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(2,-2),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(2,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-2=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(4,2),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 4=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=2(\frac{1}{4})t,\,y+2=(\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/91500faad34245d5b2389ae71aa39f34b10b9a75b1b75307b5aa6231b311307b.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(1,2),$ and passes through the point $(7,-4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,-4),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=-4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ -6=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ -6 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ -6 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(-\frac{3}{2})t,\,y-2=(-\frac{3}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-3t,\,y-2=-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(-2,3)$ and which passes through the point $(-10,-5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-10,-5),$ we can substitute $x=-10$ and $y=-5$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8=2pt \\ -8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =p{(-\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ -8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\frac{2}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-3=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-3=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/34e9beebbecc3eff77faa9b01f4684e334ec7cbdcbd9b00e328f95f7be88c1d4.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-2,4),$ and passes through the point $(2,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,4),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-4=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(2,2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-4=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-4=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+4)^{2}=-3(x-3)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-3)^{2}=-12(x-5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(5,3).$ So we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p(x-5) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p & =-12 \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(-3){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=-3{t}^{2},\,y-3=-6t.
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+2)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(x+5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(-5,-2).$ So we have

$$
x+5=p{t}^{2},\,y+2=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =\frac{1}{2}(x+5) \\ 4p(x+5) & =\frac{1}{2}(x+5) \\ 4p & =\frac{1}{2} \\ p & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+5=(\frac{1}{8}){t}^{2},\,y+2=2(\frac{1}{8})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+5=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2},\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}t.
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-1)^{2}=-5(x-1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,1).$ So we have

$$
x-1=p{t}^{2},\,y-1=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p(x-1) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p & =-5 \\ p & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=(-\frac{5}{4}){t}^{2},\,y-1=2(-\frac{5}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-\frac{5}{4}{t}^{2},\,y-1=-\frac{5}{2}t.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(5,-1),$ and passes through the point $(17,11).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(5,-1),$ and so we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y+1=2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(17,11),$ we can substitute $x=17$ and $y=11$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}12=p{t}^{2} \\ 12=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =2pt \\ 6 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{6}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =p{(\frac{6}{p})}^{2} \\ 12 & =p\cdot \frac{36}{{p}^{2}} \\ 12 & =\frac{36}{p} \\ p & =\frac{36}{12} \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(3){t}^{2},\,y+1=2(3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=3{t}^{2},\,y+1=6t.
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Consider the following parametric equation of the parabola 

$$
x-1=3t,\,y+4={t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this parabola is

$(x\,-$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{x-1}{3},\,{t}^{2}=y+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-1}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=y+4$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9} & =y+4 \\ {(x-1)}^{2} & =9(y+4)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Consider the following parametric equation of the parabola 

$$
x-4=3{t}^{2},\,y+2=6t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this parabola is

$(y\,+$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{x-4}{3},\,t=\frac{y+2}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{y+2}{6})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{x-4}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{36} & =\frac{x-4}{3} \\ (y+2)^{2} & =36\cdot (\frac{x-4}{3}) \\ (y+2)^{2} & =12(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-6=3t,\,y-3=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{x-6}{3},\,{t}^{2}=\frac{2(y-3)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-6}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{2(y-3)}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{9} & =\frac{2(y-3)}{3} \\ (x-6)^{2} & =9\cdot (\frac{2(y-3)}{3}) \\ (x-6)^{2} & =6(y-3).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x+1=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+2=\frac{3}{2}t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{4(x+1)}{3},\,t=\frac{2(y+2)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{2(y+2)}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4(y+2)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{4(x+1)}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4(y+2)^{2}}{9} & =\frac{4(x+1)}{3} \\ (y+2)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}\cdot (\frac{4(x+1)}{3}) \\ (y+2)^{2} & =3(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
canonical_examples.problem:
What set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in(-\infty, \infty),$ generates the parabola shown below?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/1a75a5242f3636efac8def7fc62458e1c1c6972ca79a1ab6fd73af47be622a7a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-4,5),$ and passes through the point $(-2,3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = 2pt, \qquad y - k = pt^2,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-4,5),$ and so we have

$$
x + 4 = 2pt, \qquad y - 5 = pt^2.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-2, 3),$ we can substitute $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x + 4 = 2\left(-\dfrac12\right)t, \qquad y - 5 = \left(-\dfrac12\right)t^2 ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x + 4 = -t, \qquad y - 5 = -\dfrac12t^2 .
$$

Example: 
                    Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
canonical_examples.problem:
What set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in(-\infty,\infty),$ generates the parabola shown below?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/8355891fbc605593a32dd100ee8c1c2e4324da0630755984158ec23f6d419ab9.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(-3,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,0).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = pt^2, \qquad y - k = 2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-3,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+3 = pt^2, \qquad y-2 = 2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,0),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=p{t}^{2} \\ -2=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(-\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t^2, \qquad y -2 = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+3 = \dfrac{1}{4}t^2, \qquad y -2= \dfrac{1}{2}t .
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Cartesian Equation of Parabola Given Its Parametric Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-1 = -2t^2, \qquad y+1 = -4t, \qquad t\in(-\infty, \infty).
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-\frac{x-1}{2},\,t=-\frac{y+1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{y+1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation $t^2 = -\dfrac{x-1}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16} & =-\frac{x-1}{2} \\ (y+1)^{2} & =16\cdot (-\frac{x-1}{2}) \\ (y+1)^{2} & =-8(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Justification That the Parametric Equations Describe a Parabola
tutorials.problem:
Let's recall the parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k){:}$

$$
x-h = 2pt, \qquad y-k = pt^2, \qquad t\in(-\infty,\infty).
$$

How can we be sure that these equations describe a parabola?

First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-h & =2pt & ⟹ &  & t & =\frac{x-h}{2p} \\ y-k & =p{t}^{2} & ⟹ &  & {t}^{2} & =\frac{y-k}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first equation above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-h}{2p})}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{4{p}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting in the second equation $t^2 = \dfrac{y-k}{p},$ we can eliminate the parameter $t$ and rearrange to find the Cartesian equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{4{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{y-k}{p} & =\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{4{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{y-k}{p}\cdot 4{p}^{2} & =(x-h)^{2} \\ (x-h)^{2} & =4p(y-k)\end{aligned}
$$

This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical parabola with vertex $(h,k).$ Therefore, the parametric equations do indeed describe a vertical parabola.

If we did the same for the parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k),$ we would obtain the Cartesian equation of a horizontal parabola, namely $(y-k)^2 = 4p(x-h).$

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (1,−2) and which passes through the point (−3,6)?

a
x−1=t,y+2=12t2
b
x+3=2t,y−6=t2
c
x+1=t2,y−2=12t
d
x−3=−t,y+6=−2t2
e
x−1=12t2,y+2=t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(1,−2), and so we have

x−1=2pt,y+2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (−3,6), we can substitute x=−3 and y=6 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{−4=2pt8=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

−4=2ptt=−2p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

8=p(−2p)28=p⋅4p28=4pp=12.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−1=2(12)t,y−(−2)=(12)t2, which simplify to

x−1=t,y+2=12t2.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(2,-2),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(2,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-2=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(4,2),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 4=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=2(\frac{1}{4})t,\,y+2=(\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x−2=12t,y+2=14t2
b
x−2=14t,y+2=12t2
c
x−2=12t,y+2=12t2
d
x+2=14t,y−2=12t2
e
x+2=14t,y−2=14t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (2,−2), and passes through the point (4,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(2,−2), and so we have

x−2=2pt,y+2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (4,2), we can substitute x=4 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{2=2pt4=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

2=2pt1=ptt=1p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

4=p(1p)24=p⋅1p24=1pp=14.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−2=2(14)t,y+2=(14)t2,

which simplify to

x−2=12t,y+2=14t2.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(1,2),$ and passes through the point $(7,-4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,-4),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=-4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ -6=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ -6 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ -6 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(-\frac{3}{2})t,\,y-2=(-\frac{3}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-3t,\,y-2=-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x+1=−43t,y+2=−23t2
b
x−1=−43t,y−2=−23t2
c
x+1=−3t,y+2=−32t2
d
x−1=−3t,y−2=−32t2
e
x−1=−32t,y−2=−32t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (1,2), and passes through the point (7,−4).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(1,2), and so we have

x−1=2pt,y−2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (7,−4), we can substitute x=7 and y=−4 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{6=2pt−6=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

6=2ptt=3p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−6=p(3p)2−6=p⋅9p2−6=9pp=−32.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−1=2(−32)t,y−2=(−32)t2,

which simplify to

x−1=−3t,y−2=−32t2.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-10,-5),$ we can substitute $x=-10$ and $y=-5$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8=2pt \\ -8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =p{(-\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ -8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\frac{2}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-3=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-3=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (−2,3) and which passes through the point (−10,−5)?

a
x+2=−2t,y−3=−t2
b
x+2=−4t,y−3=−2t2
c
x−2=−4t,y−3=−2t2
d
x+2=−4t,y+3=−2t2
e
x+2=−t,y−3=−12t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,3), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−3=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (−10,−5), we can substitute x=−10 and y=−5 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{−8=2pt−8=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

−8=2ptt=−4p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−8=p(−4p)2−8=p⋅16p2−1=2pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−3=(−2)t2, which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−3=−2t2.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-2,4),$ and passes through the point $(2,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,4),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-4=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(2,2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-4=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-4=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2
b
x+2=4t,y−4=2t2
c
x+4=2t,y−2=−t2
d
x+4=−2t2,y−2=−t
e
x−2=−4t2,y+4=−2t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (−2,4), and passes through the point (2,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,4), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−4=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (2,2), we can substitute x=2 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{4=2pt−2=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

4=2pt2=ptt=2p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−2=p(2p)2−2=p⋅4p2−2=4pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−4=(−2)t2,

which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(-3,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,0).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x - h = pt^2, \qquad y - k = 2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k) = (-3,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+3 = pt^2, \qquad y-2 = 2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,0),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=0$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=p{t}^{2} \\ -2=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(-\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t^2, \qquad y -2 = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)t ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+3 = \dfrac{1}{4}t^2, \qquad y -2= \dfrac{1}{2}t .
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+4)^{2}=-3(x-3)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y+4)2=−3(x−3)?

a
x−3=−32t2,y+4=−3t
b
x+4=−t2,y−3=−6t
c
x+4=−6t2,y−3=−t
d
x−3=−34t2,y+4=−32t
e
x−3=−3t2,y+4=−6t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(3,−4). So we have

x−3=pt2,y+4=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−3(x−3)4p(x−3)=−3(x−3)4p=−3p=−34.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−3=(−34)t2,y+4=2(−34)t,

which simplify to

x−3=−34t2,y+4=−32t.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(5,3).$ So we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p(x-5) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p & =-12 \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(-3){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=-3{t}^{2},\,y-3=-6t.
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y−3)2=−12(x−5)?

a
x−5=3t2,y−3=−12t
b
x−5=−3t2,y−3=3t
c
x+5=−t2,y+3=6t
d
x−5=−3t2,y−3=−6t
e
x+5=−4t2,y+3=12t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(5,3). So we have

x−5=pt2,y−3=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−12(x−5)4p(x−5)=−12(x−5)4p=−12p=−3.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−5=(−3)t2,y−3=2(−3)t,

which simplify to

x−5=−3t2,y−3=−6t.

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(-5,-2).$ So we have

$$
x+5=p{t}^{2},\,y+2=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =\frac{1}{2}(x+5) \\ 4p(x+5) & =\frac{1}{2}(x+5) \\ 4p & =\frac{1}{2} \\ p & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+5=(\frac{1}{8}){t}^{2},\,y+2=2(\frac{1}{8})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+5=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2},\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}t.
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y+2)2=12(x+5)?

a
x+5=12t2,y+2=t
b
x−5=14t2,y−2=18t
c
x−5=2t2,y−2=t
d
x+5=18t2,y+2=14t
e
x+5=t2,y+2=2t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(−5,−2). So we have

x+5=pt2,y+2=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=12(x+5)4p(x+5)=12(x+5)4p=12p=18.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+5=(18)t2,y+2=2(18)t,

which simplify to

x+5=18t2,y+2=14t.

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,1).$ So we have

$$
x-1=p{t}^{2},\,y-1=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p(x-1) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p & =-5 \\ p & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=(-\frac{5}{4}){t}^{2},\,y-1=2(-\frac{5}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-\frac{5}{4}{t}^{2},\,y-1=-\frac{5}{2}t.
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y−1)2=−5(x−1)?

a
x+1=52t2,y+1=52t
b
x−1=−52t2,y−1=−54t
c
x−1=−54t2,y−1=−52t
d
x−1=52t2,y−1=54t
e
x−1=−52t,y−1=−54t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(1,1). So we have

x−1=pt2,y−1=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−5(x−1)4p(x−1)=−5(x−1)4p=−5p=−54.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−1=(−54)t2,y−1=2(−54)t,

which simplify to

x−1=−54t2,y−1=−52t.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(5,-1),$ and passes through the point $(17,11).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(5,-1),$ and so we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y+1=2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(17,11),$ we can substitute $x=17$ and $y=11$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}12=p{t}^{2} \\ 12=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =2pt \\ 6 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{6}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =p{(\frac{6}{p})}^{2} \\ 12 & =p\cdot \frac{36}{{p}^{2}} \\ 12 & =\frac{36}{p} \\ p & =\frac{36}{12} \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(3){t}^{2},\,y+1=2(3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=3{t}^{2},\,y+1=6t.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-\frac{x-1}{2},\,t=-\frac{y+1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{y+1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation $t^2 = -\dfrac{x-1}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{16} & =-\frac{x-1}{2} \\ (y+1)^{2} & =16\cdot (-\frac{x-1}{2}) \\ (y+1)^{2} & =-8(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

x+1=34t2,y+2=32t,t∈(−∞,∞).

a
(y−2)2=32(x−1)
b
(y+2)2=3(x+1)
c
(y−2)2=3(x−1)
d
(y+2)2=32(x+1)
e
(y+2)2=13(x+1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's make t the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

t2=4(x+1)3,t=2(y+2)3.

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

t2=(2(y+2)3)2=4(y+2)29.

We can now eliminate the parameter t by substituting the above into the equation t2=4(x+1)3 and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

4(y+2)29=4(x+1)3(y+2)2=94⋅(4(x+1)3)(y+2)2=3(x+1).

tutorial.problem:
Let's recall the parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k){:}$

$$
x-h = 2pt, \qquad y-k = pt^2, \qquad t\in(-\infty,\infty).
$$

How can we be sure that these equations describe a parabola?

First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-h & =2pt & ⟹ &  & t & =\frac{x-h}{2p} \\ y-k & =p{t}^{2} & ⟹ &  & {t}^{2} & =\frac{y-k}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first equation above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-h}{2p})}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{4{p}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting in the second equation $t^2 = \dfrac{y-k}{p},$ we can eliminate the parameter $t$ and rearrange to find the Cartesian equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{4{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{y-k}{p} & =\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{4{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{y-k}{p}\cdot 4{p}^{2} & =(x-h)^{2} \\ (x-h)^{2} & =4p(y-k)\end{aligned}
$$

This is the Cartesian equation of a vertical parabola with vertex $(h,k).$ Therefore, the parametric equations do indeed describe a vertical parabola.

If we did the same for the parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k),$ we would obtain the Cartesian equation of a horizontal parabola, namely $(y-k)^2 = 4p(x-h).$

question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(1,-2)$ and which passes through the point $(-3,6)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-3,6),$ we can substitute $x=-3$ and $y=6$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4=2pt \\ 8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(-\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-(-2)=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (1,−2) and which passes through the point (−3,6)?

a
x−1=t,y+2=12t2
b
x+3=2t,y−6=t2
c
x+1=t2,y−2=12t
d
x−3=−t,y+6=−2t2
e
x−1=12t2,y+2=t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(1,−2), and so we have

x−1=2pt,y+2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (−3,6), we can substitute x=−3 and y=6 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{−4=2pt8=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

−4=2ptt=−2p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

8=p(−2p)28=p⋅4p28=4pp=12.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−1=2(12)t,y−(−2)=(12)t2, which simplify to

x−1=t,y+2=12t2.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-3,6),$ we can substitute $x=-3$ and $y=6$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4=2pt \\ 8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(-\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-(-2)=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4=2pt \\ 8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(-\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

x-1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-(-2)=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
question.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(2,-2),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(2,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-2=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(4,2),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 4=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=2(\frac{1}{4})t,\,y+2=(\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x−2=12t,y+2=14t2
b
x−2=14t,y+2=12t2
c
x−2=12t,y+2=12t2
d
x+2=14t,y−2=12t2
e
x+2=14t,y−2=14t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (2,−2), and passes through the point (4,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(2,−2), and so we have

x−2=2pt,y+2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (4,2), we can substitute x=4 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{2=2pt4=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

2=2pt1=ptt=1p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

4=p(1p)24=p⋅1p24=1pp=14.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−2=2(14)t,y+2=(14)t2,

which simplify to

x−2=12t,y+2=14t2.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(2,-2),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(2,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-2=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(4,2),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 4=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=2(\frac{1}{4})t,\,y+2=(\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x−2=12t,y+2=14t2
b
x−2=14t,y+2=12t2
c
x−2=12t,y+2=12t2
d
x+2=14t,y−2=12t2
e
x+2=14t,y−2=14t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (2,−2), and passes through the point (4,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(2,−2), and so we have

x−2=2pt,y+2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (4,2), we can substitute x=4 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{2=2pt4=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

2=2pt1=ptt=1p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

4=p(1p)24=p⋅1p24=1pp=14.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−2=2(14)t,y+2=(14)t2,

which simplify to

x−2=12t,y+2=14t2.
question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola

solution.reasoning: The graph has vertex (2,-2) and passes through (4,2), so y+2=A(x-2)^2 with 4=4A, giving A=1. Option a has t=2(x-2), hence y+2=t^2/4=(x-2)^2, and all real t cover the full parabola. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked solution belongs to another example.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/d963d5620df91a05c8371ef09beeb84546c5f5a8cda047f2c2c3b9933f3d5c01.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
feedback.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(2,-2),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(2,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-2=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(4,2),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 4=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 4 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=2(\frac{1}{4})t,\,y+2=(\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 2

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x−2=12t,y+2=14t2
b
x−2=14t,y+2=12t2
c
x−2=12t,y+2=12t2
d
x+2=14t,y−2=12t2
e
x+2=14t,y−2=14t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (2,−2), and passes through the point (4,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(2,−2), and so we have

x−2=2pt,y+2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (4,2), we can substitute x=4 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{2=2pt4=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

2=2pt1=ptt=1p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

4=p(1p)24=p⋅1p24=1pp=14.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−2=2(14)t,y+2=(14)t2,

which simplify to

x−2=12t,y+2=14t2.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162956/assets/91500faad34245d5b2389ae71aa39f34b10b9a75b1b75307b5aa6231b311307b.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
question.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(1,2),$ and passes through the point $(7,-4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,-4),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=-4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ -6=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ -6 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ -6 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(-\frac{3}{2})t,\,y-2=(-\frac{3}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-3t,\,y-2=-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x+1=−43t,y+2=−23t2
b
x−1=−43t,y−2=−23t2
c
x+1=−3t,y+2=−32t2
d
x−1=−3t,y−2=−32t2
e
x−1=−32t,y−2=−32t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (1,2), and passes through the point (7,−4).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(1,2), and so we have

x−1=2pt,y−2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (7,−4), we can substitute x=7 and y=−4 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{6=2pt−6=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

6=2ptt=3p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−6=p(3p)2−6=p⋅9p2−6=9pp=−32.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−1=2(−32)t,y−2=(−32)t2,

which simplify to

x−1=−3t,y−2=−32t2.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(1,2),$ and passes through the point $(7,-4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,-4),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=-4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ -6=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ -6 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ -6 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(-\frac{3}{2})t,\,y-2=(-\frac{3}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-3t,\,y-2=-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x+1=−43t,y+2=−23t2
b
x−1=−43t,y−2=−23t2
c
x+1=−3t,y+2=−32t2
d
x−1=−3t,y−2=−32t2
e
x−1=−32t,y−2=−32t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (1,2), and passes through the point (7,−4).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(1,2), and so we have

x−1=2pt,y−2=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (7,−4), we can substitute x=7 and y=−4 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{6=2pt−6=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

6=2ptt=3p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−6=p(3p)2−6=p⋅9p2−6=9pp=−32.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−1=2(−32)t,y−2=(−32)t2,

which simplify to

x−1=−3t,y−2=−32t2.

solution.reasoning: The vertex is (1,2), so y-2=A(x-1)^2. The point (7,-4) gives -6=36A, hence A=-1/6. Option d eliminates t to give y-2=-(x-1)^2/6; t=-2 produces (7,-4), and all real t cover the full parabola. The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(7,-4),$ we can substitute $x=7$ and $y=-4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ -6=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ -6 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ -6 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(-\frac{3}{2})t,\,y-2=(-\frac{3}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-3t,\,y-2=-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

x−1=2pt,y−2=pt2.

{6=2pt−6=pt2.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(-2,3)$ and which passes through the point $(-10,-5)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-10,-5),$ we can substitute $x=-10$ and $y=-5$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8=2pt \\ -8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =p{(-\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ -8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\frac{2}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-3=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-3=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (−2,3) and which passes through the point (−10,−5)?

a
x+2=−2t,y−3=−t2
b
x+2=−4t,y−3=−2t2
c
x−2=−4t,y−3=−2t2
d
x+2=−4t,y+3=−2t2
e
x+2=−t,y−3=−12t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,3), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−3=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (−10,−5), we can substitute x=−10 and y=−5 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{−8=2pt−8=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

−8=2ptt=−4p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−8=p(−4p)2−8=p⋅16p2−1=2pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−3=(−2)t2, which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−3=−2t2.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-10,-5),$ we can substitute $x=-10$ and $y=-5$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8=2pt \\ -8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =p{(-\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ -8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\frac{2}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-3=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-3=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (−2,3) and which passes through the point (−10,−5)?

a
x+2=−2t,y−3=−t2
b
x+2=−4t,y−3=−2t2
c
x−2=−4t,y−3=−2t2
d
x+2=−4t,y+3=−2t2
e
x+2=−t,y−3=−12t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,3), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−3=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (−10,−5), we can substitute x=−10 and y=−5 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{−8=2pt−8=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

−8=2ptt=−4p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−8=p(−4p)2−8=p⋅16p2−1=2pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−3=(−2)t2, which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−3=−2t2.
question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola

solution.reasoning: The vertex gives y-3=A(x+2)^2. Substituting (-10,-5) yields -8=64A, so A=-1/8. Option b eliminates t to give y-3=-(x+2)^2/8; t=2 produces (-10,-5), and all real t cover the full parabola. feedback.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(-2,3)$ and which passes through the point $(-10,-5)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-10,-5),$ we can substitute $x=-10$ and $y=-5$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8=2pt \\ -8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =p{(-\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ -8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\frac{2}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-3=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-3=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

question.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-2,4),$ and passes through the point $(2,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,4),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-4=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(2,2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-4=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-4=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2
b
x+2=4t,y−4=2t2
c
x+4=2t,y−2=−t2
d
x+4=−2t2,y−2=−t
e
x−2=−4t2,y+4=−2t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (−2,4), and passes through the point (2,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,4), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−4=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (2,2), we can substitute x=2 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{4=2pt−2=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

4=2pt2=ptt=2p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−2=p(2p)2−2=p⋅4p2−2=4pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−4=(−2)t2,

which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-2,4),$ and passes through the point $(2,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,4),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-4=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(2,2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-4=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-4=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the parabola shown above?

a
x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2
b
x+2=4t,y−4=2t2
c
x+4=2t,y−2=−t2
d
x+4=−2t2,y−2=−t
e
x−2=−4t2,y+4=−2t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (−2,4), and passes through the point (2,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,4), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−4=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (2,2), we can substitute x=2 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{4=2pt−2=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

4=2pt2=ptt=2p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−2=p(2p)2−2=p⋅4p2−2=4pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−4=(−2)t2,

which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2.
question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola

solution.reasoning: The vertex is (-2,4), so y-4=A(x+2)^2. Substituting (2,2) gives -2=16A, hence A=-1/8. Option a eliminates t to give y-4=-(x+2)^2/8; t=-1 produces (2,2), and all real t cover the full parabola. feedback.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-2,4),$ and passes through the point $(2,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,4),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y-4=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(2,2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=2pt \\ -2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ -2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-2)t,\,y-4=(-2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-4t,\,y-4=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

x+4=−2t2,y−2=−t
e
x−2=−4t2,y+4=−2t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at (−2,4), and passes through the point (2,2).

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=2pt,y−k=pt2,

where p is constant.

In our case, (h,k)=(−2,4), and so we have

x+2=2pt,y−4=pt2.

Since the parabola passes through (2,2), we can substitute x=2 and y=2 into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

{4=2pt−2=pt2.

Solving the first equation for t, we have

4=2pt2=ptt=2p.

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for p, we get

−2=p(2p)2−2=p⋅4p2−2=4pp=−2.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x+2=2(−2)t,y−4=(−2)t2,

which simplify to

x+2=−4t,y−4=−2t2.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+4)^{2}=-3(x-3)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y+4)2=−3(x−3)?

a
x−3=−32t2,y+4=−3t
b
x+4=−t2,y−3=−6t
c
x+4=−6t2,y−3=−t
d
x−3=−34t2,y+4=−32t
e
x−3=−3t2,y+4=−6t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(3,−4). So we have

x−3=pt2,y+4=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−3(x−3)4p(x−3)=−3(x−3)4p=−3p=−34.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−3=(−34)t2,y+4=2(−34)t,

which simplify to

x−3=−34t2,y+4=−32t.

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y+4)2=−3(x−3)?

a
x−3=−32t2,y+4=−3t
b
x+4=−t2,y−3=−6t
c
x+4=−6t2,y−3=−t
d
x−3=−34t2,y+4=−32t
e
x−3=−3t2,y+4=−6t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(3,−4). So we have

x−3=pt2,y+4=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−3(x−3)4p(x−3)=−3(x−3)4p=−3p=−34.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−3=(−34)t2,y+4=2(−34)t,

which simplify to

x−3=−34t2,y+4=−32t.
question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola

solution.reasoning: For option d, (y+4)^2=9t^2/4 and -3(x-3)=9t^2/4, so it satisfies the required Cartesian equation. Since y+4=-3t/2 ranges over all real numbers, it generates the full parabola. Option a instead gives (y+4)^2=-6(x-3). No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked solution concerns a different example.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y+4)^{2}=-3(x-3)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(3,-4).$ So we have

$$
x-3=p{t}^{2},\,y+4=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p(x-3) & =-3(x-3) \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-3=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+4=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-3=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2},\,y+4=-\frac{3}{2}t.
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-3)^{2}=-12(x-5)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(5,3).$ So we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p(x-5) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p & =-12 \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(-3){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=-3{t}^{2},\,y-3=-6t.
$$

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y−3)2=−12(x−5)?

a
x−5=3t2,y−3=−12t
b
x−5=−3t2,y−3=3t
c
x+5=−t2,y+3=6t
d
x−5=−3t2,y−3=−6t

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

x−5=pt2,y−3=2pt.

4p(x−h)=−12(x−5)4p(x−5)=−12(x−5)4p=−12p=−3.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−5=(−3)t2,y−3=2(−3)t,

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(5,3).$ So we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p(x-5) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p & =-12 \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(-3){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=-3{t}^{2},\,y-3=-6t.
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for t∈(−∞,∞), generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation (y−3)2=−12(x−5)?

a
x−5=3t2,y−3=−12t
b
x−5=−3t2,y−3=3t
c
x+5=−t2,y+3=6t
d
x−5=−3t2,y−3=−6t
e
x+5=−4t2,y+3=12t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola (y−k)2=4p(x−h) that has its vertex at (h,k) are

x−h=pt2,y−k=2pt,

where p is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(5,3). So we have

x−5=pt2,y−3=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−12(x−5)4p(x−5)=−12(x−5)4p=−12p=−3.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−5=(−3)t2,y−3=2(−3)t,

which simplify to

x−5=−3t2,y−3=−6t.
question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Horizontal Parabola

solution.reasoning: Option d gives (y-3)^2=36t^2 and -12(x-5)=36t^2, exactly the required equation. Since y-3=-6t ranges over all real numbers, it generates the full parabola. Option b instead gives (y-3)^2=-3(x-5). No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked solution concerns a different example.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-3)^{2}=-12(x-5)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(5,3).$ So we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p(x-5) & =-12(x-5) \\ 4p & =-12 \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(-3){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=-3{t}^{2},\,y-3=-6t.
$$

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case (y−k)2=4p(x−h), we see that the parabola has its vertex at (h,k)=(5,3). So we have

x−5=pt2,y−3=2pt.

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for p, we get

4p(x−h)=−12(x−5)4p(x−5)=−12(x−5)4p=−12p=−3.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

x−5=(−3)t2,y−3=2(−3)t,

which simplify to

x−5=−3t2,y−3=−6t.
